summary:
Trend Detective is a web app that helps anyone find out whether Earth's climate is really changing where they live. It shows 14 Earth system variables, including temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, evaporation, runoff and aerosols. The data comes from NASA's MERRA-2, GLDAS and GPM IMERG products, averaged over each of the 84 states of Mexico and the United States and shown on an interactive 3D globe.

Users pick a state and a variable, either by tapping the globe or through a guided "detective mode" that asks three plain-language questions. The app then shows the annual time series with its trend line and answers three questions: is it rising, falling or can't we tell? By how much per decade? And how strong is the evidence? All statistics are computed in our data pipeline: a Theil-Sen slope with its confidence interval and a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation. Two states can also be compared to test whether their trends differ.

This matters because trends are often misread. Trend Detective never presents "not enough evidence" as "no change," and it never suggests a cause. Every result shows its period, sample size, method and data source (product, version and DOI), so students, citizens and scientists can trust and check what they see.
details:
What it does and how it works

Trend Detective is a web app that answers one question: is the climate really changing in a given place? It covers the 84 states of Mexico and the United States and 14 Earth system variables: air temperature (mean, maximum and minimum), precipitation, soil moisture, soil temperature, evapotranspiration, runoff, snow water equivalent, specific humidity, total precipitable water, total ozone, aerosol optical depth and dust optical depth.

The project has two parts:

1. A Python data pipeline. It downloads monthly NASA data (MERRA-2, GLDAS Noah and GPM IMERG) from GES DISC through earthaccess. It averages each grid over each state, weighting every cell by the fraction of its area that falls inside the state. It then builds annual series and precomputes trends for every time window of at least 10 years between 1980 and 2025. Trends use a Theil-Sen slope with its confidence interval and a Mann-Kendall significance test corrected for autocorrelation. The pipeline also tests whether the trends of two states differ. We cross-checked regional averages against NASA Giovanni and tested our Mann-Kendall code against an independent library.

2. A web interface. Users pick a state on an interactive 3D globe, with a search box or from a table, then choose a variable and a period. The app shows a clear verdict (rising, falling, or not enough evidence), the change per decade with its interval, the p-value, a plain-language sentence, and the annual series with its trend line. A "detective mode" asks three simple questions (what are you curious about, where, and what do you think happened), runs a real analysis, and compares the user's guess with the result.

Benefits

- It turns thousands of NASA files into answers that take seconds to read, with no programming or GIS skills needed.

- It works on phones and still runs without 3D graphics support, falling back to search and a table.

- Each view is saved in the URL, so a link reproduces the exact analysis.

- Every number can be traced to its source: product, version, DOI, access date, method and sample size.

Intended impact

We want students, teachers and curious citizens to explore NASA Earth data about the places they care about, and to learn how to read a trend correctly: how big it is, how sure we are, and why a trend does not prove a cause. The same tool also gives researchers and decision-makers a quick, transparent first look at regional change.

Tools and technologies

- Data and science: Python, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, xarray, h5netcdf/h5py, Shapely, earthaccess, pytest and pymannkendall (used only as a cross-check).

- NASA data: MERRA-2 (M2TMNXSLV, M2SMNXSLV, M2TMNXAER), GLDAS Noah 2.1 (GLDAS_NOAH025_M) and GPM IMERG Final (GPM_3IMERGM), with NASA Giovanni for validation.

- Web: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, react-globe.gl with three.js, d3-scale and d3-shape, Vitest and oxlint.

- Hosting: a static site on Vercel. The browser does no statistics; it only reads precomputed JSON files.

- Workflow: Git and GitHub, specification-driven development with GitHub Spec Kit, and AI-assisted coding with Claude Code. Team members reviewed and tested every feature.

How it is creative

- Detective mode turns data exploration into a guessing game: users predict first, then check their guess against real NASA data.

- The globe lets users compare the same variable across neighboring states and see the challenge's key point: one process can push a variable up in one region and down in another.

- Precomputing every window of 10 or more years makes changing the period instant, without any server.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: "not enough evidence" is never shown as "no change," and the app never suggests a cause or a forecast. It uses robust methods that suit short, autocorrelated climate series.

- Clarity for non-experts: plain language, a verdict shown with both an icon and a word, and terms explained where they appear.

- Accessibility and reach: a mobile-first layout, a table alternative to the globe, and no heavy backend.

- Reproducibility: pinned software versions, documented data provenance, automated tests, and validation against Giovanni.
dataRefs: NASA GES DISC (Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center)
NASA Giovanni (used to validate regional averages)
NASA Earthdata Search and CMR (Common Metadata Repository)
earthaccess (NASA Openscapes Python library for Earthdata access)
